quests.definition: Location contrast: 'Here' indicates proximity to the speaker; 'There' marks distance away from the speaker.
quests.example: Please come over here and sit next to me.
quests.usageExample: Put the delivery boxes over there near the garage.
quests.nativeTip: 'Here' is anchored to the speaker's current spot. 'There' always points outward to another location.
quests.visualAnchor: 📍 HERE = Right with speaker | 🗺️ THERE = Away at a distance
quests.commonMistake: Don't confuse 'there' (location) with 'their' (possessive) or 'they're' (they are).

quests.definition: Action direction: 'Give' transfers an item outward to another; 'Take' brings an item inward into your own possession.
quests.example: She wants to give you a birthday present.
quests.usageExample: Take an umbrella with you in case it rains.
quests.nativeTip: 'Give' is generous and outward; 'Take' is acquiring and inward. In social settings, 'give and take' denotes compromise.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎁 GIVE = Outward to others | 🤲 TAKE = Inward to self
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'give a picture' when you capture one on camera — say 'take a picture'.

quests.definition: Spatial orientation: 'Right' is the side of most people's dominant writing hand; 'Left' is the opposite side toward the heart.
quests.example: Turn right at the traffic lights.
quests.usageExample: He wears his watch on his left wrist.
quests.nativeTip: 'Right' also means correct or just in other contexts, but spatially its absolute opposite is 'left'.
quests.visualAnchor: ➡️ RIGHT = Eastward / Clockwise | ⬅️ LEFT = Westward / Counterclockwise
quests.commonMistake: 'Left' is also the past tense of 'leave', but as a direction it strictly opposes 'right'.

quests.definition: Quality & Ethics: 'Good' signifies desirable, beneficial, or high standard; 'Bad' marks undesirable, harmful, or inferior quality.
quests.example: Eating fresh fruit is good for your health.
quests.usageExample: Spoiled milk has a very bad smell.
quests.nativeTip: English uses 'well' for health and manner ('I feel well'), but 'good' for inherent quality ('This soup is good').
quests.visualAnchor: ⭐ GOOD = Positive & Desirable | ❌ BAD = Negative & Harmful
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'I did good on the test' in formal English — say 'I did well on the test'.

quests.definition: Frequency of occurrence: 'Ever' means at any point in time; 'Never' means at zero points in time (not ever).
quests.example: Have you ever seen the northern lights?
quests.usageExample: I have never tasted caviar in my life.
quests.nativeTip: 'Never' is already negative ('not + ever'). Never use a double negative like 'I don't never go'.
quests.visualAnchor: ⏳ EVER = Any point in time | 🚫 NEVER = Zero points in time
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'I haven't never' — always say 'I have never' or 'I haven't ever'.

quests.definition: Ordinal sequence: 'First' precedes all others in a series; 'Last' concludes all others with none remaining behind.
quests.example: She crossed the finish line in first place.
quests.usageExample: He was the last student to leave the classroom.
quests.nativeTip: 'At first' means initially; 'at last' means finally after waiting. Notice how the opposites produce opposite idioms!
quests.visualAnchor: 🥇 FIRST = Head of the line | 🏁 LAST = Tail of the line
quests.commonMistake: Don't confuse 'last' (final) with 'latest' (most recent, with more expected to come).

quests.definition: Solar rhythm: 'Day' is the illuminated period between sunrise and sunset; 'Night' is the dark period under moonlight.
quests.example: The sun shines brightly throughout the day.
quests.usageExample: The stars are clearly visible at night.
quests.nativeTip: Native speakers say 'by day' and 'at night' (notice the preposition shift!). Also, 'day and night' signifies nonstop effort.
quests.visualAnchor: ☀️ DAY = Sunlight & Activity | 🌙 NIGHT = Darkness & Rest
quests.commonMistake: Say 'in the morning' or 'in the daytime', but always 'at night' (not 'in the night' for general habits).

quests.definition: Magnitude of physical scale: 'Big' exceeds average size or impact; 'Little' is limited or below average in size or count.
quests.example: They bought a big house with a huge garden.
quests.usageExample: A little bird landed right on the windowsill.
quests.nativeTip: 'Little' often carries an affectionate tone ('my little brother', 'a little gift'), while 'small' is purely factual.
quests.visualAnchor: 🐘 BIG = Immense size | 🐥 LITTLE = Tiny & endearing
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'a few water' — use 'a little water' for uncountable nouns.

quests.definition: Territorial presence: 'Home' is your own residence or home stadium; 'Away' is off your ground, in distant territory.
quests.example: After a long trip, it feels wonderful to be home.
quests.usageExample: Our soccer team played an away game in Chicago.
quests.nativeTip: In sports and travel, 'home and away' defines where matches happen. 'Away' requires movement or distance from home base.
quests.visualAnchor: 🏡 HOME = Native territory | ✈️ AWAY = Distant / Foreign ground
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'I go to home' — say 'I go home' (no preposition needed with home as adverb).

quests.definition: Gender contrast: 'Man' denotes an adult human male; 'Woman' denotes an adult human female.
quests.example: The tall man held the door open for the guests.
quests.usageExample: The woman was elected mayor of the city.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the irregular plurals: one man / two men (/mɛn/), one woman / two women (/ˈwɪmɪn/). Pronunciation changes drastically!
quests.visualAnchor: 👨 MAN = Adult male | 👩 WOMAN = Adult female
quests.commonMistake: Watch the plural spelling and vowel: 'women' is pronounced 'WIM-in', never 'WOM-en'.

quests.definition: Identity & uniqueness: 'Same' means identical or unchanged; 'Other' denotes different, distinct, or alternative.
quests.example: We both ordered the exact same coffee.
quests.usageExample: If that table is taken, let us choose the other one.
quests.nativeTip: 'Same' almost always takes the definite article ('the same'). 'Other' points to the alternative item.
quests.visualAnchor: 🪞 SAME = Identical twin | 🔀 OTHER = Distinct alternative
quests.commonMistake: Always say 'the same as' (never 'the same than' or 'the same with').

quests.definition: Parental lineage: 'Father' is a male parent; 'Mother' is a female parent.
quests.example: His father taught him how to play guitar.
quests.usageExample: Her mother works as a pediatric surgeon.
quests.nativeTip: Informal pairs follow parallel symmetry: Dad ↔ Mom, Papa ↔ Mama. In idioms, 'necessity is the mother of invention'.
quests.visualAnchor: 👨‍👧 FATHER = Paternal parent | 👩‍👧 MOTHER = Maternal parent
quests.commonMistake: Capitalize Father and Mother only when using them directly as proper names: 'Ask Mother' vs 'my mother'.

quests.definition: Process dynamic: 'Start' initiates motion or an activity; 'Stop' brings movement or action to an end.
quests.example: The race will start as soon as the whistle blows.
quests.usageExample: Please stop the car before reaching the crosswalk.
quests.nativeTip: Both words can be followed by verbs with -ing: 'start running', 'stop running'. But 'stop to run' means halting in order to run!
quests.visualAnchor: 🟢 START = Green light / Initiate | 🔴 STOP = Red light / Cease
quests.commonMistake: Remember: 'stop doing' = quit the action; 'stop to do' = pause what you are doing in order to do something else.

quests.definition: Youth gender: 'Girl' is a female child or adolescent; 'Boy' is a male child or adolescent.
quests.example: The little girl wore a bright yellow raincoat.
quests.usageExample: The boy rode his bicycle across the park.
quests.nativeTip: Used informally by adults among peers ('girls' night out', 'the boys'), but in professional settings use 'women' and 'men'.
quests.visualAnchor: 👧 GIRL = Young female | 👦 BOY = Young male
quests.commonMistake: Refer to adult professionals as women and men, reserving girl and boy for young children.

quests.definition: Kinetic state: 'Move' means changing position, travelling, or relocating; 'Stay' means remaining rooted in one place.
quests.example: Do not move while the doctor takes the X-ray.
quests.usageExample: You should stay indoors during the heavy snowstorm.
quests.nativeTip: 'Stay' can mean temporary lodging ('stay at a hotel') as well as physical stillness ('stay still').
quests.visualAnchor: 🏃 MOVE = Kinetic motion | 🧘 STAY = Stillness & rootedness
quests.commonMistake: Don't confuse 'stay' (remain) with 'live' (permanent residence).

quests.definition: Outcome of competition: 'Lost' indicates defeat or forfeiture; 'Won' denotes victory, triumph, or securing a prize.
quests.example: Our team lost the final match by just one goal.
quests.usageExample: She won the championship trophy after months of training.
quests.nativeTip: Pronunciation tip: 'Won' is pronounced exactly like the number 'one' (/wʌn/), never with an 'o' sound.
quests.visualAnchor: 🥈 LOST = Defeated | 🏆 WON = Victorious champion
quests.commonMistake: Never pronounce 'won' with the sound of 'on' — it sounds identical to 'one' (/wʌn/).

quests.definition: Biological vitality: 'Live' (/laɪv/ as adj) possesses organic life or active energy; 'Dead' is completely devoid of life.
quests.example: We watched the concert on live television.
quests.usageExample: The winter cold left the garden plants completely dead.
quests.nativeTip: Pay attention to part of speech: 'live' /laɪv/ is the adjective (opposing 'dead'), while 'alive' /əˈlaɪv/ is also its opposite.
quests.visualAnchor: 🌱 LIVE = Vibrant vitality | 🍂 DEAD = Inanimate / Depleted
quests.commonMistake: Don't confuse the verb 'to live' /lɪv/ with the adjective 'live' /laɪv/.

quests.definition: Countable quantity: 'Many' specifies a large number of discrete items; 'Few' marks a small, scarce number of countable items.
quests.example: There are many historical monuments in Rome.
quests.usageExample: Very few people attended the morning lecture.
quests.nativeTip: 'Many' and 'few' are STRICTLY for countable nouns (books, people). For uncountable nouns (water, money), use 'much' and 'little'.
quests.visualAnchor: 👥 MANY = Crowded abundance | 👤 FEW = Scarce countable number
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'few water' or 'many time' — use 'little water' and 'much time' for uncountable things.

quests.definition: Status in sports/rules: 'Safe' means reaching a base without being tagged; 'Out' means retired or eliminated from play.
quests.example: The umpire raised his arms and yelled, 'Safe!'
quests.usageExample: Three strikes and the batter is out.
quests.nativeTip: While 'safe' generally opposes 'dangerous', in baseball and gaming rulebooks, 'safe' directly opposes 'out'!
quests.visualAnchor: 🛡️ SAFE = Secured base | ❌ OUT = Eliminated from play
quests.commonMistake: In sports terminology, 'out' means disqualified from active turn, while 'safe' protects your score.

quests.definition: Cognitive retention: 'Remember' retains or retrieves facts from memory; 'Forget' fails to retain or recall them.
quests.example: Always remember to lock the front door.
quests.usageExample: I often forget where I placed my car keys.
quests.nativeTip: 'Remember to do' looks to future duty; 'remember doing' recalls a past event. 'Forget' behaves identically!
quests.visualAnchor: 💡 REMEMBER = Recalled to mind | 🌫️ FORGET = Slipped from mind
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'I remind where I parked' — say 'I remember where I parked' ('remind' needs an object: 'remind me').

quests.definition: Emotional polarity: 'Love' is profound affection, adoration, and care; 'Hate' is intense hostility, detestation, and aversion.
quests.example: I absolutely love spending time with my family.
quests.usageExample: He hates waking up before sunrise on cold mornings.
quests.nativeTip: In everyday English, native speakers exaggerate with both: 'I'd love some tea' (keen preference) vs 'I hate traffic' (strong annoyance).
quests.visualAnchor: ❤️ LOVE = Deep affection & care | 💔 HATE = Intense aversion & dislike
quests.commonMistake: Be cautious when using 'hate' with people in formal speech — native speakers soften it with 'I don't particularly enjoy'.

quests.definition: Target contact: 'Hit' strikes the intended target with accuracy; 'Miss' fails to reach, strike, or catch the target.
quests.example: The archer managed to hit the exact center of the bullseye.
quests.usageExample: If you drive too slowly, you will miss the morning train.
quests.nativeTip: Idiom alert: 'hit or miss' means unpredictable or variable in quality ('The restaurant food is hit or miss').
quests.visualAnchor: 🎯 HIT = Bullseye contact | 💨 MISS = Passed by without contact
quests.commonMistake: 'Miss' also means feeling longing for someone ('I miss you'), but in targeting it directly opposes 'hit'.

quests.definition: Offspring gender: 'Daughter' is a female human child; 'Son' is a male human child.
quests.example: Their oldest daughter just graduated from medical school.
quests.usageExample: He took his son to his first professional baseball game.
quests.nativeTip: 'Son' is pronounced identically to 'sun' (/sʌn/). In legal or formal records, children are listed as 'sons and daughters'.
quests.visualAnchor: 👧 DAUGHTER = Female child | 👦 SON = Male child
quests.commonMistake: Don't confuse the spelling of 'son' with 'sun' (in the sky), although they sound 100% identical.

quests.definition: Possession status: 'Find' discovers or recovers an object; 'Lose' misplaces, forfeits, or fails to retain an item.
quests.example: Did you find your missing house keys under the couch?
quests.usageExample: Be very careful not to lose your passport at the airport.
quests.nativeTip: Remember the spelling: 'lose' (/luːz/ with one 'o' = misplace) vs 'loose' (/luːs/ with two 'o's = not tight).
quests.visualAnchor: 🔍 FIND = Recover & discover | ❓ LOSE = Misplace & forfeit
quests.commonMistake: Never write 'I don't want to loose my keys' — it is always 'lose' with one 'o'.

quests.definition: Access state: 'Open' allows entry, exit, or airflow; 'Shut' is completely closed, preventing passage.
quests.example: Please leave the window open to let in fresh morning air.
quests.usageExample: He shut the heavy iron gate behind him.
quests.nativeTip: 'Shut' is more abrupt and complete than 'close'. 'Shut your mouth' is blunt, while 'keep eyes shut' emphasizes tight closure.
quests.visualAnchor: 🚪 OPEN = Unobstructed access | 🔒 SHUT = Blocked & sealed
quests.commonMistake: 'Shut' has the same form in past tense: 'He shut the door yesterday' (never 'shutted').

quests.definition: Matrimonial role: 'Husband' denotes a married man; 'Wife' denotes a married woman.
quests.example: She and her husband have been married for twenty years.
quests.usageExample: His wife is an accomplished concert violinist.
quests.nativeTip: Plural of 'wife' follows the f -> ves rule: one wife, two wives (/waɪvz/). The gender-neutral term is 'spouse'.
quests.visualAnchor: 🤵 HUSBAND = Married man | 👰 WIFE = Married woman
quests.commonMistake: Always spell the plural of wife as 'wives', never 'wifes'.

quests.definition: Sibling relation: 'Brother' is a male sibling sharing parents; 'Sister' is a female sibling sharing parents.
quests.example: My brother is two years older than I am.
quests.usageExample: She called her sister to share the exciting news.
quests.nativeTip: The umbrella term for brothers and sisters is 'siblings' ('Do you have any siblings?').
quests.visualAnchor: 👦 BROTHER = Male sibling | 👧 SISTER = Female sibling
quests.commonMistake: Don't ask 'How many brothers and sisters you have?' — ask 'How many siblings do you have?' for natural fluency.

quests.definition: Completeness & parentage: 'Whole' is 100% complete or sharing both parents; 'Half' is a 50% partition or sharing one parent.
quests.example: He ate the whole pizza by himself.
quests.usageExample: Cut the sandwich in half so we can share it.
quests.nativeTip: In family relations: a 'whole brother' shares both mother and father; a 'half brother' shares only one parent.
quests.visualAnchor: 🌕 WHOLE = 100% Undivided | 🌗 HALF = 50% Partition
quests.commonMistake: The 'l' in 'half' is completely silent (/hæf/, rhyming with 'laugh'). Never pronounce the 'l'.

quests.definition: Body posture: 'Sit' rests body weight on a seat with hips bent; 'Stand' maintains an upright posture supported by one's feet.
quests.example: Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.
quests.usageExample: The audience had to stand during the national anthem.
quests.nativeTip: Particles transform both: 'sit down', 'sit up' (erect spine), 'stand up', 'stand by' (wait / support).
quests.visualAnchor: 🪑 SIT = Seated resting posture | 🧍 STAND = Upright posture
quests.commonMistake: Notice past forms: sit -> sat, stand -> stood. Both are irregular verbs.

quests.definition: Spatial boundary: 'Inside' refers to the interior enclosed perimeter; 'Outside' refers to the external exterior environment.
quests.example: It began raining heavily, so we went inside the house.
quests.usageExample: The children are playing outside in the fresh sunshine.
quests.nativeTip: In compound adjectives: 'an inside job' (secret internal collusion) vs 'outside help' (external independent support).
quests.visualAnchor: 🏠 INSIDE = Enclosed interior | 🌳 OUTSIDE = Open exterior
quests.commonMistake: You don't need 'to' with inside/outside as adverbs: say 'go outside', not 'go to outside'.
